title: Chicken Adobo
description: Tender chicken simmered in a tangy, savory blend of soy sauce, vinegar, garlic, and peppercorns.
background: Adobo is one of the Philippines' best-loved home-cooked dishes. Every family has its own version; this comforting classic lets the vinegar and soy sauce do the talking.
steps: Combine chicken, soy sauce, and half the garlic. Marinate for at least 20 minutes, or up to overnight in the refrigerator.
Lift the chicken from the marinade. Heat the oil in a heavy pot and brown the chicken on all sides.
Add the remaining garlic, marinade, vinegar, water, bay leaves, and peppercorns. Bring to a boil without stirring.
Lower the heat, cover, and simmer for 35–40 minutes, turning the chicken once, until tender and cooked through.
Uncover and simmer until the sauce is glossy and reduced to your liking. Serve warm over rice.
tips: Let the vinegar boil before stirring to mellow its sharpness. Brown the chicken well for deeper flavor.
author: Ian's Kitchen

title: Sinigang na Baboy
description: A soul-warming tamarind broth with tender pork, tomatoes, and fresh vegetables.
background: Sinigang's bright, comforting sourness is a favorite across Filipino homes. Serve a steaming bowl with rice and fish sauce on the side.
ingredients: 1 kg pork belly or ribs, cut into pieces
1 packet tamarind soup mix, or 1 cup tamarind extract
steps: Bring pork and water to a boil in a large pot. Skim off any foam, then add the onion and tomatoes.
Cover and simmer gently for 50–60 minutes, until the pork is tender.
Stir in the tamarind and fish sauce. Add the radish and cook until nearly tender.
Add the eggplant and green peppers; simmer for 5 minutes.
Stir in the kangkong and cook just until wilted. Taste the broth and adjust the sourness and seasoning.
tips: Keep the broth at a gentle simmer for a clear, flavorful soup. Add leafy greens just before serving.
author: Ian's Kitchen

title: Kare-Kare
description: Slow-cooked oxtail and vegetables in a rich, mellow peanut sauce, served with bagoong.
background: Kare-kare is a celebratory Filipino stew with a velvety peanut sauce. Bagoong on the side adds the salty, savory contrast that makes every bite sing.
steps: Place oxtail, water, and onion in a pot. Bring to a boil, skim, and simmer until very tender, about 2 hours. Reserve the broth.
Whisk peanut butter and toasted rice flour into 3 cups of warm broth until smooth.
Return the mixture to the pot and simmer, stirring, until thick and creamy. Season to taste.
Blanch the sitaw, eggplant, banana blossom, and pechay until just tender.
Arrange the meat and vegetables in the sauce. Serve with warm rice and bagoong.
tips: A pressure cooker can shorten the oxtail cooking time. Keep the bagoong on the side so everyone can season to taste.
author: Ian's Kitchen

title: Tinolang Manok
description: A light and fragrant chicken soup with ginger, green papaya, and leafy moringa.
background: Gentle ginger broth, tender chicken, and a bowl of rice make tinola the kind of comforting meal Filipinos turn to on any day.
ingredients: 1 whole chicken, cut into serving pieces
1 small green papaya, peeled and sliced
2 cups chili leaves or moringa leaves
steps: Heat oil in a pot. Sauté the onion, garlic, and ginger until fragrant.
Add the chicken and fish sauce. Cook, turning the pieces, until lightly browned.
Pour in water or broth. Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer for 30 minutes.
Add the green papaya and cook until tender, about 10 minutes.
Stir in the leaves and cook just until wilted. Taste and season with fish sauce.
tips: Green papaya is traditional, but chayote is an easy-to-find substitute. Add the leaves at the very end.
author: Ian's Kitchen

title: Pancit Canton
description: Springy noodles tossed with crisp vegetables, savory sauce, and tender chicken.
background: A celebratory noodle dish at birthdays and family gatherings, pancit canton is a delicious way to feed a crowd.
steps: Stir together the chicken broth, soy sauce, and oyster sauce.
Heat oil in a wok. Sauté the garlic and onion, then cook the chicken until no longer pink.
Add the carrot and cabbage. Stir-fry for 2 minutes, then pour in the sauce mixture.
Add the noodles and toss gently until they've absorbed the sauce and are tender. Add a splash of water if needed.
Serve with calamansi wedges.
tips: Keep the noodles moving in the wok so they cook evenly. A squeeze of calamansi brightens the whole dish.

title: Halo-Halo
description: A joyful tower of crushed ice, sweet beans, jellies, fruit, leche flan, and purple yam.
background: Halo-halo means mix-mix. This cool, colorful dessert is endlessly customizable and perfect for warm afternoons.
ingredients: 1/2 cup nata de coco or coconut jelly
steps: Divide the beans, jackfruit, nata de coco, and kaong between two tall glasses.
Pile shaved ice generously on top of the sweet ingredients.
Pour evaporated milk over each glass.
Top each with ube ice cream, a slice of leche flan, and toasted rice flakes.
Serve immediately with a long spoon, and mix everything together before eating.
tips: Chill the glasses first to keep the ice from melting too quickly. Add your favorite sweet preserves.
author: Ian's Kitchen

title: Leche Flan
description: Silky steamed custard with a golden caramel top and a soft, delicate wobble.
background: A fixture at Filipino celebrations, leche flan turns a few simple pantry ingredients into a special-occasion dessert.
steps: Warm sugar and water in a small pan until the sugar melts and turns amber. Pour carefully into a llanera or small heatproof mold.
Whisk egg yolks gently with condensed milk, evaporated milk, and vanilla until combined. Avoid whisking in too much air.
Strain the custard into the caramel-lined mold and cover tightly with foil.
Steam over gently simmering water for 40–45 minutes, until just set in the center.
Cool completely, then chill for at least 4 hours. Run a knife around the edge and invert onto a serving plate.
tips: Straining the custard helps create a smooth texture. Keep the steam gentle to avoid bubbles.
